# §7.3 The Method of Laplace Transform: Direct Incorporation of Initial Conditions, Cramer’s Rule, and Delayed Forcing

In solving systems of differential equations, the operator method of §7.2 offers an elegant algebraic framework for deriving complementary solutions with arbitrary constants before enforcing initial data. However, the primary operational complication of the operator method is that decoupled scalar equations generate \(2N\) constants, requiring the elimination of \(N\) redundant constants by substituting back into the coupled differential system. For initial value problems (IVPs), the **Laplace transform method** bypasses this elimination step completely. By applying the derivative property \(\mathcal{L}\{\dot{x}\} = sX(s) - x(0)\), initial conditions are absorbed directly into the algebraic right-hand side on the very first step. The system is thereby transformed into an algebraic matrix equation in terms of rational functions in \(s\), where Cramer’s rule isolates the unique solution immediately without generating excess arbitrary constants.

> **MENTAL MODEL:** The Laplace transform moves differential systems from the continuous flow of time into a static algebraic balance in the \(s\)-domain. While derivatives in the time domain couple rates of change, in the \(s\)-domain initial states \(x(0), y(0)\) enter like external sources (virtual impulses) appended directly to the right-hand side. Solving the system decouples the response into two autonomous domains: the **Zero-Input Response (ZIR)** driven purely by initial energy, and the **Zero-State Response (ZSR)** driven purely by external forcing.

---

## 7.3.1 Transformation of Linear Differential Systems into the s-Domain

Consider a general first-order initial value problem with constant coefficients in two dependent variables:

$$\begin{cases} a_{11}\dot{x} + b_{11}x + a_{12}\dot{y} + b_{12}y = f_1(t) \\ a_{21}\dot{x} + b_{21}x + a_{22}\dot{y} + b_{22}y = f_2(t) \end{cases}, \quad x(0) = x_0, \; y(0) = y_0$$

Taking the term-by-term Laplace transform of both equations brings the derivative operational properties into action:

$$\mathcal{L}\{\dot{x}(t)\} = sX(s) - x(0), \quad \mathcal{L}\{\ddot{x}(t)\} = s^2X(s) - sx(0) - \dot{x}(0)$$

Applying this rule scales \(x(0)\) and \(y(0)\) by their respective coefficients, collecting them alongside the input transforms \(F_1(s)\) and \(F_2(s)\) on the right-hand side. The system assumes a linear algebraic matrix form in \(s\):

$$\begin{bmatrix} a_{11}s + b_{11} & a_{12}s + b_{12} \\ a_{21}s + b_{21} & a_{22}s + b_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X(s) \\ Y(s) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11}x_0 + a_{12}y_0 + F_1(s) \\ a_{21}x_0 + a_{22}y_0 + F_2(s) \end{bmatrix}$$

The determinant \(\Delta(s)\) of this coefficient matrix is the exact counterpart of the characteristic polynomial \(\phi(s)\) from the operator method. The unknown transform functions \(X(s)\) and \(Y(s)\) are determined immediately by Cramer’s rule:

$$X(s) = \frac{\Delta_x(s)}{\Delta(s)}, \quad Y(s) = \frac{\Delta_y(s)}{\Delta(s)}, \quad \Delta(s) = \det[A(s)]$$

By the linearity of the right-hand side vector, the transformed solution decouples naturally into two fundamental parts:

$$X(s) = X_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(s) + X_{\mathrm{ZSR}}(s), \quad Y(s) = Y_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(s) + Y_{\mathrm{ZSR}}(s)$$

Here \(X_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(s)\) depends solely on initial conditions \(x_0, y_0\) under zero external input (\(F(s) = 0\)); while \(X_{\mathrm{ZSR}}(s)\) depends strictly on external forcing under quiescent initial conditions (\(x_0 = y_0 = 0\)).

> **PRACTICAL CHECK:** The roots of the characteristic equation \(\Delta(s) = 0\) are the poles of the system. These poles correspond identically to the characteristic roots \(\phi(\lambda) = 0\) of the operator method. Upon inverse transformation, the ZIR component contains only natural modes (\(e^{st}\)) generated by these poles; the ZSR incorporates both natural poles (transient dynamics) and forcing poles (steady-state dynamics).

---

## Example 7.11: Harmonic System with Exponential Forcing

Consider the system of Example 7.11 from the textbook:

$$\begin{cases} \dot{x} - 3x - 6y = 0 \\ 3x + \dot{y} + 3y = 18te^{-3t} \end{cases}, \quad x(0) = 1, \; y(0) = 0$$

Taking the Laplace transform of each equation with \(\mathcal{L}\{18te^{-3t}\} = \frac{18}{(s + 3)^2}\) and initial data \(x(0) = 1, y(0) = 0\):

$$\begin{bmatrix} s - 3 & -6 \\ 3 & s + 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X(s) \\ Y(s) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \frac{18}{(s + 3)^2} \end{bmatrix}$$

The system characteristic determinant is:

$$\Delta(s) = (s - 3)(s + 3) + 18 = s^2 + 9 = (s + 3i)(s - 3i)$$

The pure imaginary poles \(s = \pm 3i\) correspond to harmonic oscillations with natural frequency \(\omega = 3\text{ rad/s}\). Evaluating Cramer numerator determinants:

$$\Delta_x(s) = (s + 3) + \frac{108}{(s + 3)^2}, \quad \Delta_y(s) = -3 + \frac{18(s - 3)}{(s + 3)^2}$$

This directly isolates \(X(s)\) and \(Y(s)\), cleanly partitioned into ZIR and ZSR components:

$$X(s) = \frac{s + 3}{s^2 + 9} + \frac{108}{(s^2 + 9)(s + 3)^2}, \quad Y(s) = -\frac{3}{s^2 + 9} + \frac{18(s - 3)}{(s^2 + 9)(s + 3)^2}$$

Inverting the first terms yields free harmonic oscillation: \(x_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t) = \cos 3t + \sin 3t\) and \(y_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t) = -\sin 3t\). Expanding the forced terms via partial fractions gives the total solution:

$$\begin{cases} x(t) = -\cos 3t + \sin 3t + 2(1 + 3t)e^{-3t} \\ y(t) = \cos 3t - (1 + 6t)e^{-3t} \end{cases}$$

Observe the crucial achievement: no arbitrary constants were introduced, and no auxiliary algebraic elimination was required! Initial values were integrated smoothly from the first step.

> **SIGN RULE:** Be meticulous with the negative sign in the derivative transform: \(\mathcal{L}\{\dot{x}\} = sX(s) - x(0)\). On the left-hand side, the \(-x(0)\) originating from the \(\dot{x}\) term moves to the right-hand side as \(+x(0)\). However, if an equation contains \(-\dot{x}\), this term transfers to the right-hand side as \(-x(0)\).

---

## 7.3.2 Delayed Forcing and the Second Shifting Theorem

In engineering systems, external loads and voltages frequently activate suddenly as step inputs or delayed pulses. Such discontinuous or translated functions are naturally modeled with the Heaviside step function \(H(t - c)\). The second shifting theorem dictates:

$$\mathcal{L}\{f(t - c)H(t - c)\} = e^{-cs}F(s), \quad \mathcal{L}^{-1}\{e^{-cs}F(s)\} = f(t - c)H(t - c)$$

Here the exponential factor \(e^{-cs}\) represents a phase lag in the frequency domain, and ensures the response remains identically zero until \(t = c\) in the time domain.

---

## Example 7.12: Coupled Derivatives with Delayed Sinusoidal Forcing

In Example 7.12, derivatives are coupled and forcing activates at \(t = \pi\) as a sinusoidal wave:

$$\begin{cases} \dot{x} + 2x + 2\dot{y} + 5y = 0 \\ \dot{x} + 3\dot{y} + y = 10\sin(2t)H(t - \pi) \end{cases}, \quad x(0) = 2, \; y(0) = 1$$

To transform the delayed forcing, express \(\sin(2t)\) in powers of \(t - \pi\): \(\sin(2t) = \sin(2(t - \pi) + 2\pi) = \sin(2(t - \pi))\). Applying the second shifting theorem directly:

$$\mathcal{L}\{10\sin(2t)H(t - \pi)\} = \mathcal{L}\{10\sin(2(t - \pi))H(t - \pi)\} = \frac{20e^{-\pi s}}{s^2 + 4}$$

Transforming the coupled derivatives collects initial values on the right-hand side: equation 1 yields \(x(0) + 2y(0) = 2 + 2(1) = 4\), and equation 2 yields \(x(0) + 3y(0) = 2 + 3(1) = 5\). Setting up the matrix system:

$$\begin{bmatrix} s + 2 & 2s + 5 \\ s & 3s + 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X(s) \\ Y(s) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 + \frac{20e^{-\pi s}}{s^2 + 4} \end{bmatrix}$$

The characteristic determinant produces damped roots:

$$\Delta(s) = (s + 2)(3s + 1) - s(2s + 5) = s^2 + 2s + 2 = (s + 1)^2 + 1$$

Poles at \(s = -1 \pm i\) govern natural damped oscillations at 1 rad/s with exponential decay \(e^{-t}\). From Cramer’s rule, the Zero-Input Response is:

$$x_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t) = e^{-t}(2\cos t - 23\sin t), \quad y_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t) = e^{-t}(\cos t + 9\sin t)$$

The Zero-State Response carries the delay factor \(e^{-\pi s}\) and inverts via partial fractions into:

$$\begin{cases} x_{\mathrm{ZSR}}(t) = \left[ 14\cos 2t - 3\sin 2t + e^{-(t - \pi)}(14\cos t + 8\sin t) \right] H(t - \pi) \\ y_{\mathrm{ZSR}}(t) = \left[ -6\cos 2t + 2\sin 2t - e^{-(t - \pi)}(6\cos t + 2\sin t) \right] H(t - \pi) \end{cases}$$

Here the reductions \(\cos(t - \pi) = -\cos t\) and \(\sin(t - \pi) = -\sin t\) have been substituted. For \(t < \pi\), the system performs pure ZIR damped free vibration; at \(t = \pi\), forced oscillations activate smoothly without discontinuity.

> **COMMON PITFALL:** In delayed forcing \(\mathcal{L}\{f(t)H(t - c)\}\), the most prevalent blunder is forgetting to rewrite \(f(t)\) as a function of \(t - c\) and directly writing \(e^{-cs}F(s)\)! For instance, the transform of \(t H(t - 1)\) is NOT \(\frac{e^{-s}}{s^2}\); the function must be shifted as \(t = (t - 1) + 1\), giving \(\mathcal{L}\{(t - 1 + 1)H(t - 1)\} = e^{-s}\left(\frac{1}{s^2} + \frac{1}{s}\right)\)!

---

## Example 7.13: Second-Order Coupled System and Pole Cancellation

Example 7.13 is an asymmetric system featuring a second derivative in \(x\) and a first derivative in \(y\):

$$\begin{cases} \ddot{x} - 3\dot{x} - \dot{y} + 2y = 60t H(t - 1) \\ \dot{x} - 3x + \dot{y} = 0 \end{cases}, \quad x(0) = 5, \; \dot{x}(0) = 15, \; y(0) = 0$$

Transforming the delayed ramp \(60t H(t - 1) = 60(t - 1 + 1)H(t - 1)\):

$$\mathcal{L}\{60t H(t - 1)\} = 60e^{-s}\mathcal{L}\{t + 1\} = 60e^{-s}\left(\frac{1}{s^2} + \frac{1}{s}\right) = \frac{60(s + 1)e^{-s}}{s^2}$$

Applying Laplace transforms with \(\ddot{x} \to s^2X - 5s - 15\) and \(\dot{x} \to sX - 5\):

$$\Delta(s) = \det \begin{bmatrix} s^2 - 3s & -(s - 2) \\ s - 3 & s \end{bmatrix} = (s - 3)(s - 1)(s + 2)$$

The characteristic polynomial is 3rd degree with poles at \(s = 3, 1, -2\). When evaluating the ZIR, a remarkable algebraic cancellation occurs:

$$X_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(s) = \frac{5(s - 1)(s + 2)}{(s - 3)(s - 1)(s + 2)} = \frac{5}{s - 3} \implies x_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t) = 5e^{3t}, \quad y_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t) = 0$$

The numerator determinant factors \((s - 1)(s + 2)\) cancel the denominator poles completely! Under these initial conditions, modes \(s = 1\) and \(s = -2\) remain entirely unexcited; free vibration is pure \(e^{3t}\) while \(y_{\mathrm{ZIR}}(t)\) is identically zero.

Expanding the ZSR via partial fractions confirms that all modes are activated for \(t \ge 1\):

$$\begin{cases} x(t) = 5e^{3t} + \left( 10 + 8e^{3(t-1)} - 20e^{t-1} + 2e^{-2(t-1)} \right) H(t - 1) \\ y(t) = \left( 15 + 30t - 40e^{t-1} - 5e^{-2(t-1)} \right) H(t - 1) \end{cases}$$

---

## 7.3.3 Independent Verification and System ODE Residual Testing

> **INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION:** Analytical solutions are verified rigorously by substituting them and their derivatives back into the governing differential equations. System residuals must vanish identically to machine precision at any time \(t\):

$$E_1(t) \equiv L_1[x, y] - f_1(t) \equiv 0, \quad E_2(t) \equiv L_2[x, y] - f_2(t) \equiv 0$$

Furthermore, an independent 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) numerical integrator verifies that analytical and numerical trajectory differences remain below \(10^{-7}\).
